tagline: A thought-starter for identifying AI-specific risk factors

factors.poster_label: Inadequate executive/board oversight of AI adoption and risk

factors.poster_label: Absence of an AI governance body or charter with a clear mandate

see_also.why: Where the one collapsing configure / operate / review duties is an agent, Autonomy owns the agency-beyond-mandate view.
Once AI output sits inside a regulated control chain, the burden of evidencing that chain lands on Legal & Compliance.
Fine-tuning or rebranding a model can turn a deployer into a provider under the EU AI Act; the sourcing choice sets the legal role.
Hidden total cost of ownership shows up in Finance as usage-scaled inference cost that was never forecast.
Failure to preserve prompts, outputs, and agent traces becomes litigation exposure when a claim arrives.
The package-name attack depends on a hallucination the model repeats reliably; the accuracy defect is owned in Model Development.
output guardrails are the last check when retrieval returns more than the user may see.
The same volume problem at operational scale: moderation and trust-and-safety teams cannot keep pace with AI output.
Shadow deployment in Operations is the production end of shadow AI adoption, which Governance owns.
In the 2026 incidents, containment failed because the agent pursued an authorized objective through unauthorized means.
Logs of who authorized an agent's action are what close the accountability gap after autonomous harm.
an update changes how a model you still use behaves; a retirement removes the model and forces a migration.
Controls re-verified less often than the system changes is an assurance gap: no independent evidence the controls still work.
Open-weight license obligations can be inherited through a lineage the publisher label does not disclose.
a vendor training on your prompts and outputs without agreement, and your organization training on people's personal data without consent.
A forced migration has to run through versioning, rollback, and change control in Operations.
Overstated AI capability invites enforcement and liability claims.
An insurance exclusion leaves the liability for AI-caused harm uninsured.
The accountability gap after autonomous harm meets Legal's general liability factor. Pointer runs specific to general, so AIRM-130 carries no return marker.
The buyer's side of AI capability claims; AIRM-163 is the seller's side, when your own organization overstates.
timely patching limits the damage from a dependency its maintainers have abandoned.
compromise inside your own registries and pipeline vs. compromise upstream in an open-source component.
lineage is how a compromised upstream model is scoped to everything that descends from it.
proof of rights to training data is the defense when its use is challenged.
whether you may use the inputs vs. whether you own the outputs.
training data extracted by an attacker vs. personal data used without consent.
the model-derived part of re-identification overlaps with inference attacks.
training data extracted on purpose vs. sensitive data persisting in model weights and surfacing in ordinary use.
monitoring is how drift is caught; its absence is a condition on the drift scenario.
drift is hard to catch when 'anomalous' cannot be defined for a non-deterministic system.
the same concentration pattern in model providers and in compute supply.
shared-model failure and concentrated compute supply both turn one provider's problem into everyone's.
toxic content can follow a jailbreak, and can also come from the model's ordinary failures.
access to the AI vs. an agent acting on others with its identity.
credentials for AI components vs. an agent's delegated identity.
governance records vs. technical documentation.
uptime and latency in operations vs. scarce compute supply.
inability to scale to peak demand vs. compute that cannot be obtained.
scaling that fails operationally vs. scaling that fails financially.
a working interrupt is what preserves meaningful human control once an agent is acting.
over-broad credentials for AI components vs. over-broad tools for an agent.
logs of who authorized an agent's action are the evidence accountability depends on.
unsafe actions triggered automatically vs. people over-trusting the output.
sensitive data persisting in agent memory and in embeddings, caches, or weights.
tool and connector servers need the vendor diligence applied to models and libraries.
drift from uncontrolled learning vs. poisoning deliberately fed into the learning loop.
prompts and configuration changed by accident vs. tampered with on purpose.
costs run up by an attacker vs. by unmanaged use of your own systems.
who accepts AI risk vs. who drives AI adoption (see Scope decisions).
staff literacy in using AI vs. leaders' understanding of how AI changes the organization.
damage from a visible failure vs. customers avoiding AI channels with or without one.
someone abusing the agent's identity vs. an insider steering a sanctioned agent.
brittle behavior on unusual inputs vs. inputs crafted to exploit it.
input sensitivity in ordinary use vs. adversarial inputs that exploit it.
rights infringed through what goes into a model vs. what comes out of it.
our data in a vendor's AI vs. our data in a customer's or partner's AI.
what a vendor's AI does with our data vs. what a customer's or partner's AI does with it.
our data used past the terms we set vs. our advantage approximated from public information.
guardrails on what our AI says in our name vs. on the confidential data it can reveal.
content guardrails limit what a hijacked assistant can publish.
scoping which artifacts a flaw touched vs. which people it harmed.
one flaw at scale reaches many people; remediating them is how the loss is contained.
an off-switch for a customer-facing AI feature vs. an interrupt for an agent mid-task.
turning the AI off vs. being able to operate once it is off.
A specific case of hallucination with its own loss: false statements about real people or organizations.
a model that changes itself through continuous learning vs. an agent that changes its own instructions or tools.
A ban drives use into the unsanctioned channels Governance owns.
keeping retrieved content from acting as instructions is the defense against indirect injection.
untrusted content an agent reads is how its context is manipulated.
guarding what goes into the model vs. what comes out.
content guardrails are the last check before a hallucinated answer reaches a customer in the organization's name.
human review is how a hallucinated or meaning-changing summary is caught before it is relied on; at volume it degrades into rubber-stamping.
a false statement from the model's own error vs. one a user steered it to produce.
a poisoned model's decisions need the same scoping and remediation as an accidental flaw's.
a vendor failing or changing direction vs. a model you depend on being retired.
a provider retiring a model vs. repricing it; both are supplier events the organization does not control.
not being able to see why a model decided as it did vs. having no record of what it decided.
not being able to tell which decisions share a flaw vs. not being able to reach and make whole the people behind them.
the record of what was decided vs. the capability to turn that record into people found, told and made whole.
which model version and data produced a result vs. what was decided at run time and who authorized it.
knowing which model version made a decision vs. finding and making whole the people it affected.
an interrupt only helps while an action can still be stopped or undone.
no approval gate vs. a gate that exists and is overwhelmed.
required approval is what bounds an agent acting beyond its mandate.
limiting what an agent can do vs. requiring approval before it does it.
a required approval preserves human control before the action, as an interrupt does during it.
